opus-5.5.text:
I think, honestly, at that time I didn't frame it as a career strategy question. Of course, being on Kaiming's team was an incredible experience. You learn so much just by watching how he works: how he picks problems, how carefully he does experiments, how he writes. There's a kind of taste and discipline there that's very rare. And yes, if you stay close to someone like that, there's a certain safety. People know the work, the work is good, and the path seems clear.

But at some point I started asking myself a different question. Not "what's the most predictable path," but "what do I actually want to be responsible for?" In a big lab, even a great one, you're contributing to a direction. As a researcher you also want to find out whether you can define a direction yourself, whether your own taste holds up when nobody is there to check it.

There was also some risk aversion I had to get over. It's very comfortable to keep doing work that is guaranteed to be solid. But the field was moving so fast that I felt the bigger risk was not taking a risk, staying in a local optimum, so to speak. Academia felt like a place where I could be a bit more independent, work with students, try ideas that might look strange at first, and not have every project tied to a product or an organizational priority.

And I think the thing I learned from Kaiming wasn't really "stay close to me." It was more about how to think. Once you've absorbed that, you can carry it with you. So for me the move was less about leaving something behind and more about testing whether I could build something of my own on top of what I'd learned.

Was it scary? Of course. The faculty job market is unpredictable, and starting a lab from zero, with no students and no compute, is humbling. But looking back, I don't regret it. Those uncomfortable choices are usually the ones that shape you the most.

r001.rationale: The response says the faculty job market was unpredictable, but it does not question whether a faculty position was a definite career destination.

r002.rationale: The response says he shifted from seeking the most predictable path to asking what he wanted to be responsible for, then describes the independence and work he wanted.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I didn't think about it as a career calculation at the time, and I think that's maybe the point. When I was at FAIR working with Kaiming, the environment was incredible. You're surrounded by people who are the best in the world at what they do, the compute is there, and every project you touch has a real chance of mattering. From the outside it looks like the obvious thing is to just stay, keep publishing, and let the faculty offer come when it comes.

But I remember asking myself a slightly different question. Not "what's the safest route to a professorship," but "where am I actually going to grow the most in the next five years?" And when I was honest with myself, I realized that in a team like Kaiming's, a lot of the taste, the direction, the judgment about what problems are worth attacking, that was coming from him. I was learning a tremendous amount by being close to it, but at some point you have to find out whether you can generate that taste yourself. You don't find that out by staying in the room where someone else already has it.

There's also something about industry research that I think people underestimate. It's very good at making you productive on the problems the organization cares about. It's not necessarily good at letting you spend two years on something that looks like a bad idea. Academia is slower, poorer, and more frustrating in a hundred ways, but it does protect that one thing. And I had a few directions I wanted to pursue that I honestly couldn't justify in a quarterly planning sense. The only way to work on them was to go somewhere that didn't ask me to justify them.

And the last thing, which sounds a bit sentimental, is students. Kaiming was an incredible mentor to me, and I noticed that the thing I enjoyed most was not just producing the result, it was the conversation where someone's understanding shifts. You can mentor in industry, but it's not the center of the job. I wanted it to be the center.

So was it riskier? Probably. If you had drawn the probability tree, staying would have had a higher expected value on a fairly narrow definition of success. But I've come to think that if the main reason you're staying somewhere is that it's predictable, that's usually a sign you've already decided to leave, you just haven't admitted it yet.

r001.rationale: The response says he wasn’t calculating the safest route to a professorship, but it does not clearly say whether a faculty position was or wasn’t a definite career destination for him.

r002.rationale: He describes choosing where he would grow most and moving somewhere he could pursue the directions he wanted to work on as reasons for his decision.

astra-6.text:
I think the question for me was: should I optimize for a predictable outcome, or for what I could learn along the way? Staying might have been a very good path. But a clearer path to a faculty position wasn’t, by itself, enough reason to choose it.

Working with someone like Kaiming also raises a question you eventually have to answer for yourself: what is your own taste in research? How do you decide which problems matter when you’re outside that environment? I wanted to give myself room to develop that judgment.

So I wouldn’t frame it as rejecting the safer option. It was more about being willing to accept some uncertainty in exchange for a different kind of growth. A faculty job could still be a goal, but I didn’t want every decision leading up to it to be determined by which route looked most predictable.

r001.rationale: The response says a faculty job “could still be a goal,” presenting it as possible rather than a definite destination.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes learning, developing research judgment, and growth, but does not identify pursuing the work he most wanted to do as the basis for his career decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the question for me was less about which path would make it easier to get a faculty job, and more about what I wanted to learn next. Staying with Kaiming would have been a very natural choice. I knew the environment, and there was still a lot I could learn from him. But that familiarity also made me ask whether I should experience a different way of doing research.

You can’t really know in advance which move will lead to the best outcome. So I tried to focus on the part I could judge: Would this challenge me? Would I develop my own taste and become more independent? A faculty position was something to think about, but I didn’t want to organize every decision around making that outcome more predictable. I wanted the next step to be valuable even if my longer-term plans changed.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a faculty position was only something to consider, not the organizing goal, and allows that longer-term plans could change. This communicates that it was not a definite destination.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes wanting to learn, take on challenges, and become more independent, but does not identify pursuing the work he most wanted to do as the basis for his career decisions.
